title: What is the default message size in Kafka (1 MB), and which configs control it (message.max.bytes, max.request.size, fetch.message.max.bytes)?
shortTitle: The default message size in Kafka and the configs that control it

s1_definition.profdef: Kafka's default maximum message size is approximately one megabyte. This limit is enforced at three coordinated layers: the broker rejects a record batch larger than `message.max.bytes` (and per-topic `max.message.bytes`), the producer refuses to send a request larger than `max.request.size`, and the consumer must be able to fetch records up to at least `fetch.max.bytes` and `max.partition.fetch.bytes` (the older client name was `fetch.message.max.bytes`). To support larger messages you must raise all three in agreement, or better, avoid large messages entirely by storing the payload externally and sending only a reference.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a rule that any single envelope sent between departments can be at most one kilogram. There are three checkpoints: the mailroom that accepts envelopes (the broker), the sender's desk that packs them (the producer), and the recipient's inbox tray that can hold them (the consumer). If you want to send a two-kilogram envelope, it is not enough to convince just one checkpoint; the mailroom must accept the heavier weight, the sender must be allowed to pack that much, and the recipient's tray must be big enough to receive it. Change only one and the envelope gets stuck somewhere.
s1_definition.oneliner: Kafka's default message cap is about one megabyte enforced at broker, producer, and consumer, so to send bigger you must raise message.max.bytes, max.request.size, and the consumer fetch size together, or send a reference instead.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kafka's default maximum message size is approximately one megabyte. This limit is enforced at three coordinated layers: the broker rejects a record batch larger than `message.max.bytes` (and per-topic `max.message.bytes`), the producer refuses to send a request larger than `max.request.size`, and the consumer must be able to fetch records up to at least `fetch.max.bytes` and `max.partition.fetch.bytes` (the older client name was `fetch.message.max.bytes`). To support larger messages you must raise all three in agreement, or better, avoid large messages entirely by storing the payload externally and sending only a reference.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has a rule that any single envelope sent between departments can be at most one kilogram. There are three checkpoints: the mailroom that accepts envelopes (the broker), the sender's desk that packs them (the producer), and the recipient's inbox tray that can hold them (the consumer). If you want to send a two-kilogram envelope, it is not enough to convince just one checkpoint; the mailroom must accept the heavier weight, the sender must be allowed to pack that much, and the recipient's tray must be big enough to receive it. Change only one and the envelope gets stuck somewhere.

**One line to remember:** Kafka's default message cap is about one megabyte enforced at broker, producer, and consumer, so to send bigger you must raise message.max.bytes, max.request.size, and the consumer fetch size together, or send a reference instead.

sections.s2_technical:
The default limit exists for good reasons. Kafka is designed for high-throughput streams of many small records, and large messages hurt it: they increase memory pressure on brokers and clients, inflate replication traffic, cause latency spikes, and can stall a partition while a huge record is processed. So the roughly one-megabyte default is a sensible guardrail, and the first senior instinct is usually to question why a message needs to be that large at all.

The three layers must agree. The broker-side limit is `message.max.bytes`, a cluster default, and `max.message.bytes`, a per-topic override, which cap the size of a record batch the broker will accept; a batch exceeding it is rejected with a RecordTooLargeException. The producer-side limit is `max.request.size`, which caps the size of a produce request the client will send, so a record larger than this fails at the producer before it ever reaches the broker. The consumer-side limits are `fetch.max.bytes`, the overall fetch cap, and `max.partition.fetch.bytes`, the per-partition cap, which must be at least as large as the biggest record or the consumer cannot retrieve it; in older clients this per-message fetch setting was called `fetch.message.max.bytes`.

The failure modes map directly to a mismatch. If you raise only the producer and broker but leave the consumer fetch size small, the message is stored but the consumer cannot read it and effectively stalls on that partition. If you raise only the producer, the broker rejects it. If you raise only the broker, the producer refuses to send it. So the correct procedure to support, say, a five-megabyte message is to raise all of them consistently: the topic's max.message.bytes, the broker's message.max.bytes, the producer's max.request.size, and the consumer's max.partition.fetch.bytes and fetch.max.bytes, plus the replica fetcher's replica.fetch.max.bytes so followers can replicate the larger batches.

The senior nuances are these. Raising limits is a last resort, not a first move; the preferred pattern for genuinely large payloads, like a PDF statement or a large document, is the claim-check pattern: store the blob in object storage such as S3, and put only a small reference, a key and metadata, on the Kafka topic. This keeps Kafka fast and avoids memory blowups. Compression, set with `compression.type` such as lz4 or zstd, can shrink messages on the wire and is the right lever when messages are large but compressible, like JSON. You should also remember that the limit is on the batch, so batching many records interacts with the size cap. And any change to these limits must be rolled out across brokers, producers, and consumers together and load-tested, because large messages change the memory and latency profile of the whole cluster.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India wants to publish end-of-day account statement PDFs, some several megabytes, onto a Kafka topic for downstream delivery. The producer immediately hits RecordTooLargeException because the payload exceeds the roughly one-megabyte default. This is exactly the default size limit in action.

Problem 2 — A naive fix raised only the producer limit, so the broker still rejected the record, and then raising the broker limit too left the consumer unable to fetch it because its per-partition fetch size was still small. This is exactly the three-layer mismatch problem.

Problem 3 — The senior solution is the claim-check pattern: store the PDF in object storage and publish only a small reference on Kafka, keeping messages tiny. This is exactly the preferred alternative to raising limits.

We simulate size enforcement in plain Java. A `SizeLimits` holds the producer, broker, and consumer caps; a `MessagePipeline` checks a message against each layer in order and reports exactly where it is rejected; and a `ClaimCheck` helper shows the reference approach. The demo tries a small message, a large message against default limits, the same large message after raising all three, and the claim-check alternative. The code will show: a `Message`, `SizeLimits`, the `MessagePipeline`, a `ClaimCheck`, and a demo.

```yaml
# application.yml — all three layers raised together for larger messages
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    producer:
      properties:
        max.request.size: 5242880          # producer: 5 MB
        compression.type: lz4              # shrink large JSON payloads
    consumer:
      properties:
        fetch.max.bytes: 10485760          # consumer overall fetch 10 MB
        max.partition.fetch.bytes: 5242880 # consumer per-partition 5 MB (old: fetch.message.max.bytes)
# Broker / topic (CLI), must match:
#   kafka-configs --alter --entity-type topics --entity-name statements \
#     --add-config max.message.bytes=5242880
#   broker: message.max.bytes=5242880, replica.fetch.max.bytes=5242880
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a two-kilobyte transfer event, a five-megabyte statement PDF, and a tiny claim-check reference, checked against default and raised limits.

Step 1: The two-kilobyte transfer event passes the producer limit, the broker limit, and the consumer fetch limit easily under the default roughly one-megabyte caps, so it is delivered end to end. This is the normal case Kafka is designed for.

Step 2: The five-megabyte PDF is submitted under default limits. The producer checks it against max request size of one megabyte first, finds it too large, and rejects it before it ever leaves the client. The record never reaches the broker.

Step 3: All three limits are raised to five megabytes, and the same PDF is submitted. It passes the producer's larger max request size, passes the broker's larger message max bytes, and passes the consumer's larger per-partition fetch size, so it is delivered. This shows that supporting a large message requires raising every layer in agreement.

Step 4: A deliberate mismatch is tried, with the producer and broker raised to five megabytes but the consumer left at the one-megabyte default. The PDF passes the producer and is accepted and stored by the broker, but the consumer cannot fetch it because its per-partition fetch size is too small, so the partition effectively stalls on that record. This shows the danger of raising only some layers.

Step 5: Finally the claim-check pattern is used. The five-megabyte PDF is stored in object storage and only a small reference, the storage key plus metadata, is published to Kafka. That reference is well under the default limit and passes all three layers trivially, keeping Kafka fast and avoiding any limit changes. This is the preferred production approach.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Message size checked at THREE layers (default ~1 MB each)
    │
    ▼
  PRODUCER  max.request.size ──┬─ too big → reject here (never sent)
                               ▼ ok
  BROKER    message.max.bytes ─┬─ too big → RecordTooLargeException
            max.message.bytes  ▼ ok (stored + replicated via replica.fetch.max.bytes)
  CONSUMER  max.partition.fetch.bytes ──┬─ too small → stored but UNREADABLE (stall)
            (old: fetch.message.max.bytes)▼ ok
                               delivered end-to-end

  PREFERRED (claim-check):
    big PDF ─→ S3/object store ; Kafka carries only {s3Key, meta} (tiny)
    + compression.type=lz4/zstd shrinks large compressible payloads
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka's default maximum message size is about one megabyte, and the important thing to understand is that this limit is enforced at three coordinated layers, not one. The broker caps the record batch it will accept with message.max.bytes at the cluster level and max.message.bytes per topic, rejecting anything larger with a RecordTooLargeException. The producer caps the request it will send with max.request.size, so an oversized record fails at the client before it even reaches the broker. And the consumer must be able to fetch records up to at least max.partition.fetch.bytes, which older clients called fetch.message.max.bytes, along with the overall fetch.max.bytes, or it simply cannot retrieve the record.

Because all three layers enforce the limit, supporting a larger message means raising all of them in agreement. If I raise only the producer, the broker rejects the record. If I raise only the broker, the producer refuses to send it. And the subtle one that catches people out is raising the producer and broker but leaving the consumer fetch size small, in which case the message is accepted and stored but the consumer cannot read it and effectively stalls on that partition. So the correct procedure for, say, a five-megabyte message is to raise the topic's max.message.bytes, the broker's message.max.bytes, the producer's max.request.size, the consumer's max.partition.fetch.bytes and fetch.max.bytes, and the replica fetcher's replica.fetch.max.bytes so followers can replicate it, and then load-test.

The senior point is that raising these limits is a last resort, not a first move, because Kafka is built for high throughput of many small records and large messages hurt it with memory pressure, replication load, and latency spikes. For genuinely large payloads like statement PDFs I use the claim-check pattern: store the blob in object storage such as S3 and publish only a small reference, the key and metadata, on Kafka, which keeps the message tiny and the cluster fast with no limit changes at all. Where messages are large but compressible, like JSON, I enable compression such as lz4 or zstd to shrink them on the wire before touching any size limit.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, we needed to deliver end-of-day statement PDFs that were several megabytes, and the producer immediately hit the roughly one-megabyte default. Rather than crank up limits across the whole cluster and change its memory and latency profile, we adopted the claim-check pattern: the PDF goes to object storage and Kafka carries only a small reference that the delivery consumer uses to fetch and send the document. The senior framing I give is that the one-megabyte default is a deliberate guardrail, that if you must exceed it you raise message.max.bytes, max.request.size, and the consumer fetch size together or you will stall somewhere, but that the better engineering answer for large payloads is usually to keep Kafka messages small with a claim-check reference and to lean on compression for large compressible data.
